title: Cosmos-PLV
body:
Which robot-learning checkpoint should I evaluate next, and why?
Nebius x NVIDIA Global AI Hackathon 2026 - Physical AI track

Dashboard clips are real screen recordings of the running application
(live metric script, live Cosmos3-Edge, live Nebius call); speed-ups are labelled.

caption: Problem: offline losses do not tell checkpoints apart, and every closed-loop rollout costs robot time. 93 retrained Diffusion Policy checkpoints, 4,650 simulator rollouts.
Pipeline: cheap PLV screening -> real robosuite rollouts -> NVIDIA Cosmos3-Edge (local GPU) + NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL served by Nebius Token Factory.
Live dashboard: the pick, the free latest-epoch baseline, each rule's measured regret, and a judge-trust warning for strong checkpoints (from the pre-registered c1 audit).
Cheap screening runs the ORIGINAL PLV script on this checkpoint (Action L1, open-loop smoothness) - live, 2.5x speed.

labels: epoch 100: picks and places (sim label: success)
caption: Real simulator rollouts recorded by the pipeline (robosuite / MuJoCo, 10 fps, 2x speed); privileged labels are used only as ground truth.
Rollout viewer: real episode video, verified simulator outcome, and Cosmos3-Edge's per-keyframe answers to the task-free question 'where is the can?' (1.5x).
Live: NVIDIA Cosmos3-Edge on the local RTX 3090 (load + 8 keyframes, 2x speed). A fixed rule turns visual states into grasp / drop / success.
Live: the same episode goes to NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL on Nebius Token Factory; request id, latency and tokens are logged as evidence.
Results on 330 real rollouts: Nemotron judges success with 0.964 accuracy, Cosmos3-Edge 0.918. Failure TYPES are not solved (below a majority baseline).

When can you trust the judge? Pre-registered audits: judges cannot tell when a replan helps (r1), and they accept failures that end at the goal bin, so strong checkpoints look better than they are (c1).
The blind spot: a can in the wrong compartment (left) is a simulator failure, but Nemotron calls it a success - and still accepts 24 of 33 such cans when the prompt states the compartment.
Using the verdicts to self-train (s2, pre-registered): 36 human demos add +8 points; Nemotron-filtered self-data costs 10 points, because the blind spot let 58 failures into the training set.
Measured cost: about 2-3 s per episode per judge. All 7,003 logged Nebius calls of the project cost about $5 at the catalog price.

title: What we learned (all measured)
body:
+ Zero-shot NVIDIA judges replace a privileged success detector: 0.92-0.96 accuracy from video.
+ Adaptive allocation needs 2-3x fewer rollouts; early abort saves 16-20% robot time.
- No PLV metric beats the free 'latest epoch' pick in these runs.
- Judges miss near-goal failures, so strong checkpoints look better than they are.
- Self-training on their verdicts cost 10 points: audit the judge before you train on it.
Models: nvidia/Cosmos3-Edge (local), nvidia/Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL (Nebius Token Factory).
